text: Your toddler is building sentences of two to three words like "want more milk" or "daddy go work." Repeat their phrases back in full sentences to model language growth.
Stacking six or more blocks is a great milestone at this age. Celebrate the tower — and the crash — equally.
Your toddler is beginning to sort objects by shape and color. Try a simple sorting game with socks or toy animals.
Parallel play — playing beside but not with other kids — is completely normal right now. Cooperative play develops gradually over the next year.
Encourage your toddler to try turning door knobs and unscrewing lids. These fine motor challenges build hand strength and coordination.
Your toddler may start to show a preference for one hand over the other. This is a natural part of brain development — no need to encourage either hand.
Simple pretend play — like feeding a doll or talking on a toy phone — shows your toddler is developing symbolic thinking, a key cognitive leap.
Your toddler can likely follow two-step instructions like "pick up the ball and bring it to me." Practice with fun tasks during daily routines.
Scribbling is pre-writing. Give your toddler large crayons and big paper — they may start making deliberate vertical and horizontal lines.
If your toddler gets frustrated easily, it's because their desires outpace their abilities. Naming their emotions — "You're frustrated!" — helps build emotional vocabulary.
Walking up stairs while holding the railing is a big accomplishment at this age. Let them practice on safe, short flights.
Toddlers at this age love to imitate household tasks. Letting them "help" sweep or wipe builds confidence and motor skills.
Your toddler may begin to recognize themselves in photos and mirrors. This self-awareness is a major cognitive milestone.
Jumping with both feet off the ground usually emerges around this age. Encourage it on soft surfaces — it builds core strength and balance.
Most toddlers this age need 11-14 hours of total sleep per day, including one nap. If bedtime is a battle, the nap may need to be shortened or moved earlier.
A consistent bedtime routine — bath, book, song, sleep — signals to your toddler's brain that it's time to wind down. Keep it under 30 minutes.
Night waking can resurface around this age due to new fears or developmental leaps. Offer brief, calm reassurance without starting new habits.
If your toddler is climbing out of the crib, it may be time to transition to a toddler bed. Place the mattress low and use guardrails for safety.
Separation anxiety at bedtime is still common. A special lovey or small blanket can provide comfort and make the transition to sleep easier.
Avoid screens for at least one hour before bed. The blue light suppresses melatonin and makes falling asleep harder for toddlers.
Your toddler may start stalling at bedtime — asking for water, another story, one more hug. Set clear limits with warmth: one book, one hug, then goodnight.
If nap time is getting harder, try capping it at 90 minutes and ending by 3 PM to protect nighttime sleep.
A dark, cool room with white noise can make a real difference for toddler sleep. Aim for {{68-72°F|20-22°C}}.
Some toddlers develop fear of the dark around this age. A very dim nightlight can help without disrupting melatonin production.
Early morning waking before 6 AM is often caused by overtiredness. Try moving bedtime 15-30 minutes earlier for a week.
Your toddler's nap may naturally shift later. As long as they're getting one solid midday rest, the exact timing can be flexible.
If your toddler wakes crying from a nightmare, comfort them calmly. Nightmares can start around this age as imagination develops.
Transitioning to a big bed? Keep the rest of the sleep routine identical. Changing only one thing at a time helps toddlers adjust.
Physical activity during the day helps your toddler sleep better at night. Aim for at least an hour of active play, ideally outdoors.
Picky eating often peaks between 2 and 3 years old. Keep offering a variety of foods without pressure — repeated exposure works over time.
Your toddler can practice using a fork and spoon at most meals. Expect mess — it's how they learn to feed themselves independently.
Toddlers have small stomachs. Three meals plus two small snacks per day is usually the right rhythm — don't worry if individual meals seem tiny.
Gagging on new textures is different from choking and is quite normal. Stay calm and let your toddler work through it.
Let your toddler help with simple meal prep — washing fruit, tearing lettuce, stirring. Kids are more likely to eat food they helped prepare.
Avoid using dessert as a reward for finishing dinner. This teaches kids that sweets are more valuable than other foods.
If your toddler refuses vegetables, try serving them at the start of the meal when hunger is highest, or blend them into sauces and soups.
Water and milk are the best drinks for toddlers. Limit juice to no more than {{4 oz|120 ml}} per day, and always serve it with a meal.
Eating together as a family, even at this age, helps your toddler learn table manners and develop a healthy relationship with food.
Food jags — wanting the same food every day — are normal. Continue offering other options alongside their favorite without making it a battle.
Iron-rich foods like beans, fortified cereal, and lean meats are important at this age. Pair them with vitamin C foods to boost absorption.
Your toddler may want to pour their own drink or serve themselves. Use small, lightweight pitchers to encourage this independence safely.
Try the "division of responsibility" approach: you decide what, when, and where to eat. Your toddler decides whether and how much.
If your toddler throws food, they may be done eating or experimenting with cause and effect. Calmly end the meal rather than reacting strongly.
Check with your pediatrician to make sure your toddler's vaccinations are up to date. Some vaccines require booster doses that may be due around this age.
Hand, foot, and mouth disease is common in toddlers and usually resolves in 7-10 days. Focus on hydration and pain relief as your pediatrician advises.
Brush your toddler's teeth twice a day — morning and before bed. Let them hold a toothbrush too, but do the real brushing yourself.
Ear infections are still common at this age. Watch for ear pulling, fussiness, or trouble sleeping and contact your pediatrician.
Apply broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen 15 minutes before outdoor play. Reapply every two hours, especially after water play.
The annual flu vaccine is recommended for all children over 6 months. It's one of the best ways to protect your toddler during flu season.
Constipation is common in toddlers. Increase fiber with fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, and make sure they're drinking enough water.
Regular well-child visits during this stage are great times to discuss speech development, behavior, and any concerns about growth.
If your toddler gets frequent colds, that's actually normal — 8-10 per year is typical for young children building their immune system.
Start teaching your toddler to blow their nose by practicing blowing air out through their nostrils. It takes time but helps with congestion.
Keep a child-specific first aid kit accessible at home with bandages, saline drops, a thermometer, and any medications your pediatrician recommends.
If your toddler still uses a pacifier, now is a good time to start weaning. Prolonged use past age 2 can affect dental alignment.
Water play — pouring, splashing, filling containers — is endlessly entertaining and teaches early concepts of volume and cause and effect.
Play dough strengthens hand muscles needed for future writing. Let your toddler squeeze, roll, and poke to their heart's content.
Simple puzzles with 4-6 large pieces are perfect at this age. They build spatial awareness and problem-solving skills.
Sing songs with actions like "Itsy Bitsy Spider" or "Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes." They build vocabulary, rhythm, and body awareness all at once.
Let your toddler play in a sandbox or dirt patch. Digging and scooping are great for sensory development and motor skills.
Build an obstacle course with cushions, boxes, and tunnels. Climbing over and through objects builds gross motor skills and spatial awareness.
Your toddler may enjoy basic pretend play with a toy kitchen or toolset. Join in and follow their lead — this builds imagination and social skills.
Dancing to music helps your toddler develop rhythm, balance, and coordination. Put on different tempos and watch them move.
Reading the same book over and over is actually beneficial. Repetition helps toddlers learn new words and understand story structure.
Try finger painting with washable paints. The sensory experience is valuable even if the result is just a beautiful blob.
Simple ball games — rolling, kicking, throwing underhand — help develop coordination and teach the basics of taking turns.
Fill a bin with dried rice or pasta and hide small toys inside. This "treasure dig" builds fine motor skills and keeps toddlers engaged.
Blowing bubbles helps your toddler practice mouth control, visual tracking, and reaching — plus it's pure joy.
Give your toddler empty boxes and watch their creativity. A box can become a car, a house, or a boat — that's abstract thinking in action.
Nature walks where your toddler collects leaves, rocks, and sticks combine physical activity with sensory exploration and language building.
Your toddler can now reach higher than you think. Secure furniture to walls and move dangerous items to truly out-of-reach locations.
Never leave your toddler unattended near water — even a few inches in a bathtub or bucket can be dangerous. Drowning is silent and fast.
Your toddler should still ride rear-facing in their car seat until they reach the seat's maximum rear-facing height or weight limit.
Keep all medications, vitamins, and cleaning products locked up or out of reach. Toddlers at this age are curious and fast.
Practice holding hands in parking lots and near streets. Start teaching the concept of "we stop and look" before crossing.
Check playground equipment for hot surfaces in summer — metal slides and platforms can cause burns in direct sunlight.
Button batteries are extremely dangerous if swallowed. Keep remotes and devices with small batteries away from your toddler.
Food choking hazards at this age include whole grapes, hot dogs, popcorn, and hard candy. Cut round foods into small pieces.
If you have a pool or pond, install a four-sided fence with a self-closing gate. Pool covers alone are not a substitute for fencing.
Make sure your toddler wears a properly fitted helmet when riding a tricycle or being carried in a bike seat.
Blind cords and curtain strings are strangulation hazards. Switch to cordless window coverings or keep cords wrapped out of reach.
Teach your toddler their first name and start working on your family's last name. This is one of the earliest safety skills they can learn.
Stove knob covers are essential at this age. Your toddler may be tall enough to reach burner knobs before you realize it.
Keep a list of emergency numbers on the fridge and in your phone, including your local poison control center. You may need them quickly.
Always supervise your toddler around pets, even family pets they know well. Toddlers can move unpredictably and startle animals.
